sections.html:
Columbus city hall sends no property tax bill; the county does. Franklin County's Treasurer prints and collects it, and the Franklin County Auditor produces the valuation behind it. Part of Columbus spills into Delaware and Fairfield counties, so an address along the northern or southern fringe may answer to a different auditor and treasurer. Find the county named on your latest bill first, then make your calls.

OfficeWhat it handlesPhone and address
Franklin County AuditorValues, tax reduction applications, the Board of RevisionBoard of Revision: 614-525-3913, 373 S. High St., 20th Floor
Franklin County TreasurerMailing bills, collecting payments, penalties614-525-3438, 373 S. High St., 17th Floor, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00

Every tax year moves through the same sequence. Levies go to voters in November, the Board of Elections certifies the vote, rates get settled between the Auditor and the Ohio Department of Taxation in early December, and bills go out by mail later that month. The county tax list holds 440,173 parcels, and 239,956 of them are paid by a mortgage servicer, so plenty of owners never open a paper bill. In that case, ask the servicer for the figures before you list the house, because buyers like to see actual numbers.

Columbus owners pay a year behind. Tax year 2025 was collected in 2026, with the second half due July 20. The first half lands in late winter. The county shifted its due dates in 2026 without touching the amount owed, so go by the date printed on your own bill and not by last year's calendar.

Options include one lump sum, two halves, or monthly installments, and about 171,000 parcels use the monthly budget plan. Escrow is the owner's responsibility even when a lender handles the money, so make sure the lender's account lines up with the new dates. The Treasurer accepts mail, walk-in and online payments. A payment plan or delinquent tax contract you already have stays in force as agreed when dates move, and money paid early is credited to the account in the normal way.

Miss a deadline and ORC 323.121 adds a penalty of ten percent on the unpaid part of that half. Settle the whole amount within ten days and the penalty is cut in half. Never getting a bill does not excuse the penalty. If one has not arrived, phone 614-525-3438 and ask for the amount. It also pays to confirm the Treasurer has your current mailing address after a move.

Because the county bills a year behind, a bill that arrives after you sell can still cover months you owned the house. Ask the closing agent how the year is being split, and keep a copy of the settlement statement showing what was paid on your behalf. If you sell to a cash buyer on a short timeline, call the Treasurer early in the process so the payoff is ready before the closing date is set.

The tool is form DTE 1, a Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, filed with the Franklin County Board of Revision. This season ends March 31, 2027, and the board accepts complaints from mid-November through March 31 each year. A residential complaint comes with a Residential Data Sheet. For form questions, call the board at 614-525-3913.

Ohio reappraises every six years and updates at the halfway point. Outside those years, your value shifts only if the building is altered or torn down, or the board orders it. Evidence carries the day here. Photos of defects, an appraisal or recent nearby sales will help far more than a hunch that the number looks high.

If you win, here is how the money moves:

  • The board's decision opens a 30-day appeal window, and refund processing starts once it closes.
  • Expect the refund roughly three weeks after that, not counting mail time.
  • The refund goes to whoever paid the tax, which may be a mortgage or title company instead of you.
  • If the house has changed hands, any tax still owed on it is deducted before a refund is cut.
  • A payment made after its due date sits in the Treasurer's surplus account until the owner asks for its release.

The Auditor runs a handful of reduction programs, and every one has its own state form. Those that can apply to a Columbus house:

  • Homestead exemption for senior citizens, disabled persons and surviving spouses, form DTE 105A
  • Homestead exemption for an owner holding a total disability rating from military service, form DTE 105I
  • Owner-occupancy reduction, form DTE 105C, for a home that was the owner's primary residence when the tax year began
  • Reduction for storm or fire damage, form DTE 26
  • Current agricultural use value, form DTE 109, meant for working farmland and a poor fit for a city lot

Before listing, learn whether your parcel carries any of these. The value statement a buyer files under ORC 319.202 puts the question to the seller directly, and a yes has to be dealt with at closing. The new owner may not qualify for the same break, so the bill can climb after the sale.

sections.h2: Who handles the tax bill at a Columbus closing?
sections.html:
The title company or closing agent does. The Auditor stays out of closings and prorates nothing. The agent divides the tax year between you and the buyer and pays what is due from the proceeds. To keep that smooth, work through these steps before closing day:

  • Get a payoff figure from the Franklin County Treasurer.
  • Check the parcel for a delinquency or tax contract and tell the agent what needs clearing.
  • Mention any open Board of Revision case, since a recent sale can complicate a refund.
  • Make sure the Treasurer's mailing address is current, so the next bill finds the new owner or lender.

At transfer the seller owes the auditor's conveyance fee under ORC 319.54, which is $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater, plus any county transfer tax. After that the auditor puts the parcel in the buyer's name. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the payoff and the conveyance fee are handled the same way.

Columbus is home to roughly 938,396 people as of July 2025, which is 3.6% above its 2020 count. A typical owned home is valued at $252,900 for 2020 through 2024. Just 44.1% of homes are owner-occupied, so renters make up the majority, and median gross rent is $1,295 a month. Those are citywide figures, and one block can sit far from them. To price a particular address, get a written offer or a local appraisal, and have your latest tax bill on hand.

faqs.q: Which county bills property tax for my Columbus house?
faqs.a: Usually Franklin County, but parts of Columbus lie in Delaware and Fairfield counties. Check the last bill to see which county treasurer sent it.

faqs.q: When are Franklin County real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The second half is due July 20. The first half comes due in late winter, and its exact date is printed on your bill.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Columbus property value?
faqs.a: Yes. File form DTE 1 with the Franklin County Board of Revision before the season closes on March 31, 2027. The board's number is 614-525-3913.

faqs.q: Does the county prorate taxes when I sell?
faqs.a: No. The Auditor takes no part in closings. The title company or closing agent splits the bill between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: What if I never received a tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax is still owed and a penalty can still apply. Call the Treasurer at 614-525-3438 to get the amount.
